newsitem.title: USA: Gold prices fall 1 percent to new three-year low.
newsitem.headline: Gold prices fall 1 percent to new three-year low.

text.p: The price of gold fell more than 1 percent Friday to a new three-year low, leading other precious metals prices lower as commodity funds renewed their selling in a market still lacking players due to the New Year holidays.

"The rise of U.S. bond yields in recent days, which reduces the attractiveness of holding physical assets, and the surge in the dollar, which weakens demand for gold in other currencies, are the latest factors to weigh on precious metals prices this week," Refco New York analyst Tim Porter said.

At the Commodities Exchange, February gold tumbled $4.60 to close at $362.00 an ounce on high volume of 60,000 contracts, while in the London bullion market, spot gold fixed at its lowest levels since November 1993.

"With the U.S. stock market still strong, there's just no investment demand for gold, so gold saw its biggest one-day fall in months as commodity funds pushed the price lower," said Edward Kempf of industry consultants CPM Group.
After breaking out of its $366-370 range of the past month, longer-term gold could fall to $360 or even $340, levels last seen three years ago, analysts said.

Physical demand for gold remains weak, with CRU International reporting shipments of gold bullion into the big six import markets of Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai and Turkey, down 13 percent in the first 10 months of 1996.

Meanwhile, uncertainty about the role of gold in the new single European currency system due in 1999, and the potential for further European central bank gold sales in 1997, continues to afford the bears some protection, analysts said.

European central banks hold about 460 million ounces of gold, over 40 percent of all official holdings worldwide. But they have not decided what to do with their reserves when they surrender their monetary policy powers to the planned European central bank.
COMEX March silver ended down 4.7 cents at $4.685 an ounce Friday, while silver fixed at $4.703 in London Friday, its lowest fix since March 1995.
Silver mine output has risen 18 percent in the past four years and is projected to keep on rising in 1997 and 1998, analysts said.
COMEX warehouse silver inventories stocks, which include Wilmington Trust depositary stocks from Jan. 2, rose 600,338 ounces Thursday to 204,051,121 ounces.
Among other precious metals, NYMEX April platinum closed down $3.20 at $367.90 an ounce Friday, after platinum fixed at $366.50 an ounce in London, the lowest fix since Nov. 2, 1993.
"Production is rising steadily in southern Africa, while scrap recovery in the West continues to rise," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said.
South Africa and Russia are the world's largest producers of platinum, which is used in jewelry and in auto catalysts to reduce pollution.
"The Russians continue to sell to the West in whatever volumes they think the market will bear, while Japanese demand is falling under the impact of a depreciating currency," added Arnold.
